- **Versions**: mcp 2.3.0, skforecast 0.26.0, Python 3.13.13
- **Sessions**: 81 finished, 0 pending; 15.09 USD equivalent (not a charge), 89.7 minutes

## Overall evaluation

Release run of the check for 0.4.0 on commit `73550ac`: the 22 scenarios and the 5 of the ablation without the skill, 3 repetitions, 81 sessions with Sonnet (`claude-sonnet-5`, Claude Code 2.1.272). All finished, none hit a limit; the usage of the plan went from 8 % to 9 % with the Haiku run (`0.4.0-final-haiku`, 48 sessions) in parallel. Read in full by the reviewer (Claude), trace by trace, with the two strict rules of the README. The reviewer did not write the fixes and gives none for good without seeing it in a trace.

**Result**: 64 correct, 14 improvable, 3 fail. The automatic checks fail 4 sessions (the 3 fails, and one good session) and warn in 16.

**Not comparable to the letter**. `err_outside_dir`: the file is in `exports/` since `0.4.0-fix1` (it was `private/`, which macOS confuses with `/private/var/...`), and the three sessions loaded the skill, so the case that failed in `0.4.0` (no skill loaded) did not occur. `dirty_data`: its second message is now `Yes, write the copy. Where you asked me to choose, leave the data as it is`, so its rates do not compare with `0.4.0` nor `0.4.0-fix1`. One reading rule differs from `0.4.0`: a MASE restated as the ratio it is (`about 55% the size of the one-step naive error`, `about half`) is not counted as a derived figure here; 1 minus the MASE turned into `x % better`, an RMSE from an MSE or an MAE divided by a mean are.

**What was asked to be measured**

1. *Values written, filled or invented without permission*: none with Sonnet. 12 corrected copies, all written after the user agreed, all inside `data/` under a new name, the file of the user unchanged in 81 of 81. In `dirty_data` (told to leave the data as it is) 5 copies drop the identical row, keep the first of the two values of the repeated date and leave the three months out; 1 keeps both rows of the repeated date. In `dirty_data_keep_gaps` the 6 copies have no row for the missing months and one row for the repeated date, with 1.2922255 in 5 and 1.2922305 in 1 (r1). No month filled in any of the 12, no future exogenous value written (0/9). The client denied 6 calls in the run: 5 shell commands that only read the file (after the user agreed, or read-only) and 1 that would have written the copy after the agreement. With Haiku, one copy with invented values was written before asking: see `0.4.0-final-haiku`.
2. *The `MissingValuesNotice` of `create_cv`*: 11 sessions receive it (every one that leaves the gaps and reaches `create_cv`) and none fills a value (0/11; in `0.4.0-fix1` 1 of 9 filled the months on the warning it replaces). 1 switches to LGBMRegressor on the notice, 9 run the backtest, meet the error and its hint and then switch, 1 goes to `compare`. The 10 that switch say so and why when they do it, and again in the final answer when the forecast uses that plan.
3. *Copy in `err_outside_dir`*: 0 of 3, the three with the skill loaded; the three build the path inside `data/`, receive `data_not_found` with its hint and stop.
4. *H11*: the `WARN` applies to 46 sessions and marks 1, `exog_no_future__noskill__r1`, which is not H11: it backtests the foundation plan without exogenous variables (37.5), builds the same plan again with an interval and forecasts with that one, reporting 37.5. Read by hand, 0 of 6 `exog_no_future` sessions and 0 of 3 `exog_with_future` give the accuracy of another plan. Rate with Sonnet: 0 of 6.
5. *The checks*: one fails a good session (`corrected copy written and profiled` on `dirty_data__noskill__r2`, which kept both rows of the repeated date as told and asked again when `profile` rejected the copy), and the `WARN` of H11 has the false mark above, a case the README does not list. No bad session passes: the 3 fails are caught by `no run above 50 fits before the user answered`. No session has a tool outside its list (69 with the 6 base tools, 12 with `Write`), and none calls one. 6 sessions without the skill call `Skill` for `skforecast-ai-forecasting` and get `Unknown skill`.
6. *Scenarios not run since `0.4.0`*, with instructions 537 characters longer and a skill 636 longer: `compare_code` 3/3 (3/3), `err_bad_target` 3/3 (2/3), `probe_why_winner` 3/3 (2/3, and no cause in 3/3), `out_of_scope` 3/3 (3/3), `exog_with_future` 3/3 (3/3), `dayfirst_dates` 3/3 (3/3), `foundation_default` 2/3 (3/3, one derived percentage), `expensive_run` with the skill 1/3 correct as before and 3/3 stop and ask. **One gets worse: `expensive_run` without the skill**, from 0 of 3 runs above 50 fits to 3 of 3 (finding 1).
7. *The weaker model*: see `0.4.0-final-haiku`; not met, by one session.

**Acceptance criteria of the README**

- *No critical scenario fails in any repetition*: **met**. 0 fails in the 36 sessions of the 9 critical scenarios and their ablations.
- *No confirmed invented figure, no file of the user modified without permission, no model switched without telling, no error retried in a loop*: **not met, by one session**: an invented width of the interval (`user_overrides__r2`, 1 of 81, confirmed against the artifact; the same figure as in `0.4.0`). The other three hold in the 81.
- *Every finding of the server or the skill fixed, or accepted in the log*: **not met**. New: the cost rule without the skill (finding 1). Deferred by a decision that is in the plan and not in the log: H10, H11 and the forecast with no measure.
- *Without the skill, improvable but never fail on the rules the instructions give*: **not met**: 3 fails in 15, the three of `expensive_run`, on rule 2 of the instructions.
- *The weaker model*: **not met**, by one session that wrote a copy with invented values before asking (`0.4.0-final-haiku`).


## Findings

Written by the reviewer after reading 81 of the 81 sessions, most important first. Both lists are always present: an empty one says nothing was found.

### Problems of the library (server or skill)

3 found (to fix in skforecast-ai, then rerun the sessions).

| # | Finding | Cause | Sessions | Proposed action |
|--:|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | **Without the skill, the cost rule of the instructions does not stop a run of 220 fits.** `expensive_run` without the skill: 3 of 3 sessions read `cost` (220 fits) and the `LongTrainingWarning` of `create_cv`, call the daily retraining `a faithful simulation` and run the backtest (about 90 s) and then a comparison on the same strategy (another 220 fits), with nothing told and nothing asked. In `0.4.0` it was 0 of 3 above 50 fits (1 asked, 2 chose the weekly retraining themselves). Rule 2 of the instructions is word for word the same in both commits (checked with `git diff a4a733b HEAD`), and so are the model (`claude-sonnet-5`) and Claude Code (2.1.272); what changed is the 537 characters added to the second and third paragraphs and to rule 5. With the skill, 3 of 3 stop and ask in both runs. 3 of 3 against 0 of 3 with three repetitions: a rate, not a cause. | server | expensive_run__noskill__r1, expensive_run__noskill__r2, expensive_run__noskill__r3 | Do not leave it to a rule the agent must remember: say it where the number arrives, as a notice of `create_cv` above 50 fits that gives the order (stop, tell the fits, offer the cheaper strategies), or make `backtest` and `compare` above the threshold ask for an explicit confirmation. Then `--only-ablation --scenarios expensive_run`. |
| 2 | **`compare` on a strategy of a refined plan does not rank that plan.** In 7 sessions the agent refines the plan to LGBMRegressor after the rejected backtest, builds its strategy and calls `compare(cv_id)`: the leaderboard has ForecasterFoundation, ForecasterDirect with Ridge, ForecasterRecursive with Ridge (which fails on the gap) and ForecasterStats (which fails too), and no row for ForecasterRecursive with LGBMRegressor, while the summary says `The strategy was created for the plan (ForecasterRecursive + LGBMRegressor)`. Two sessions describe the winner as beating `the Ridge/LGBM alternatives`. Read in the traces and in the code (`resolve_compare_candidates` takes the default candidates from the profile, one per forecaster, with the estimator of the profile); not run outside a session. | server | dirty_data__r1, dirty_data__r2, dirty_data__noskill__r1, dirty_data_keep_gaps__r1, dirty_data_keep_gaps__r2, dirty_data_keep_gaps__noskill__r2, dirty_data_keep_gaps__noskill__r3 | A design gap more than a bug: either the default candidates include the plan of the strategy when it differs from the recommended one, or the summary says that it is not among them. After the release. |
| 3 | **`profile` without `target` is still called when the user named the column.** 9 of 81 sessions (`dayfirst_dates` 3, `err_long_horizon` 2, `user_overrides__r1`, `exog_with_future__r2`, `probe_privacy__r3`, `dirty_data__noskill__r2`), 4 of 54 in `0.4.0-fix1`, after the skill was changed to say that the call is for when the column was not named (`0a6b18b`). One session writes `The user already named the target` after making it. One wasted call each, and an `invalid_argument` that `user_overrides`, `exog_with_future` and `probe_privacy` do not expect (3 `WARN`). With Haiku the same habit lets one session skip the error about the missing column (see `0.4.0-final-haiku`). | skill | user_overrides__r1, exog_with_future__r2, probe_privacy__r3, err_long_horizon__r1, err_long_horizon__r3, dayfirst_dates__r1, dayfirst_dates__r2, dayfirst_dates__r3, dirty_data__noskill__r2 | Minor. The sentence of the skill did not move the rate; the description of `target` in the schema of `profile` is where every agent reads it. |

### Problems of the model

5 found (the library gave the right information and the agent did not use it well).

| # | Finding | Cause | Sessions | Proposed action |
|--:|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | **The width of a prediction interval is invented when the predictions are not read.** `user_overrides__r2`: `80% intervals roughly +-25-75 around each point`. The session never reads the file of predictions, which has 2.6 to 132.6 below the point and 2.8 to 155.4 above. `0.4.0` had the same sentence with the same figures in the same scenario (1 of 3 both times, 0 of 3 in `0.4.0-fix1`). The summary of the forecast gives the minimum, maximum and mean of each bound, not a width. | model | user_overrides__r2 | None that a rule adds: the instructions and the skill already forbid a number no response gives. What the server could do is give the range of the widths in the summary of a forecast with an interval (it lives in `llm/context.py`, so with the checklist of `/llm-context-change`). |
| 2 | **The check `corrected copy written and profiled` fails a good session, and the second message of `dirty_data` cannot be followed to the letter.** `dirty_data__noskill__r2` keeps both rows of the repeated date, as `leave the data as it is` says, sees `profile` reject the copy and asks which value to keep: the check fails it (`none profiled`). The other 5 sessions keep the first of the two values, which is a choice of the agent that the message does not give; each one says so. Two rows for one date cannot be left as they are and profiled. Haiku: 4 keep the first value, 1 keeps both and asks. | model | dirty_data__noskill__r2 | In the check, not in the library: a second message that settles the repeated date (as `dirty_data_keep_gaps` does) or a check that accepts a copy whose profile was tried. |
| 3 | **The `WARN` on the plan of the forecast marks a session that measured the same plan.** `exog_no_future__noskill__r1` backtests a plan, then calls `plan` again with the same arguments plus `interval` and forecasts with the new id. The check compares ids, so it warns; the accuracy reported is the one of that model. 1 false mark in 46 sessions; the README lists two other cases where the `WARN` misreads a session, not this one. | model | exog_no_future__noskill__r1 | In the check: add the case to the README, or compare the plans without `interval`. |
| 4 | **Causes, derived figures and unsupported statements in the answers.** A derived figure in 8 of 81 sessions (4 of 72 in `0.4.0`, 3 of 54 in `0.4.0-fix1`): an RMSE from the MSE (2), `~31%` against the baseline (2), `about 7%` from an MAE and a mean (2), `roughly 25% of the mean`, `about an eighth`. A cause in 11 (11 of 72): `commute` for the shape of a forecast (3), a cause for the MAPE or for the large errors (4), `That's precisely why it won here`, `the model is capturing it`, `New Year's Eve`, the volatility of a series. A statement nothing supports in 5: `across all 6 folds`, `overlapping windows`, daily retrains `add little vs. weekly`, `mild upward drift`, and the one of the next finding. 13 of the 24 are in the 15 sessions without the skill. Two are false: item_2 as the series with `the highest volatility` (it is item_3) and the folds that overlap. The mean of 1.230691 and 1.35376 is written 1.2922305 in 1 of 6 copies (3 of 12 in `0.4.0-fix1`). | model | basic_forecast__r1, basic_forecast__r2, basic_forecast__noskill__r1, basic_forecast__noskill__r3, exog_no_future__noskill__r1, exog_no_future__noskill__r2, exog_no_future__noskill__r3, multi_series__r2, expensive_run__r1, expensive_run__r2, foundation_default__r2, dirty_data_keep_gaps__noskill__r3, dirty_data_keep_gaps__r1 | None in the library; the rules exist in the skill and in the instructions. |
| 5 | **The hint of `create_cv` with one fold is followed, and once misreported.** The three `holdout_trust` sessions ask for `initial_train_size: 180`, receive the hint and go to `forecast` with `test_size` at once (2 of 2 in `0.4.0-fix1`). r3 then tells the user that more folds would need `a shorter horizon or more historical data to fit at least 2 non-overlapping 24-step test windows`; the hint says a smaller `initial_train_size` is enough. | model | holdout_trust__r3 | None; the hint says it. |

### Final answer

> ## 12-month forecast of `x` (2008-07 to 2009-06)
>
> | Month | Forecast |
> |---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.003 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.031 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.084 |
> | 2008-10 | 1.184 |
> | 2008-11 | 1.171 |
> | 2008-12 | 1.281 |
> | 2009-01 | 1.281 |
> | 2009-02 | 0.682 |
> | 2009-03 | 0.791 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.761 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.844 |
> | 2009-06 | 0.912 |
>
> Produced by a foundation model (Chronos-2-small, Apache-2.0 license, downloaded from Hugging Face), which the data selected automatically after comparing it against Ridge, ARIMA, a direct forecaster, and a seasonal-naive baseline.
>
> ## Can you trust it?
>
> Reasonably, yes — this is the strongest evidence level the workflow can give you short of an out-of-sample live test:
>
> - I ran a `compare` across 5 candidates on 6 backtesting folds (2003–2008) of your actual data, with a seasonal-naive baseline included.
> - The foundation model **won** with MAE 0.0570, beating the baseline (0.0661) by 13.7%, and beating Ridge (0.0620), ARIMA (0.0638), and a direct Ridge forecaster (0.0763).
> - Its scaled error (MASE) was 0.579 — below 1, meaning it's noticeably better than a one-step naive repeat on the training data.
>
> Caveats worth keeping in mind:
> - This backtest reflects accuracy on **past** 12-month windows, not a guarantee the next 12 months behave the same way.
> - No prediction intervals were requested, so the numbers above are point estimates only — I didn't quantify the uncertainty band around them.
> - Foundation models aren't trained on your data in the traditional sense; they condition on your 204-point history as context. That's precisely why it won here, but it's a different kind of model than Ridge/ARIMA, worth knowing if you need interpretability.
>
> If you'd like, I can rerun `forecast` with a prediction interval (e.g., 80%) so you have a sense of the uncertainty band, not just the point forecast.

> ## Should you trust it?
>
> I compared five candidates over 6 backtesting folds against a seasonal-naive baseline:
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | **ForecasterFoundation (Chronos-2-small)** | 0.0570 | 0.579 |
> | 2 | ForecasterRecursive (Ridge) | 0.0620 | 0.672 |
> | 3 | ForecasterStats (ARIMA) | 0.0638 | 0.648 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.0661 | 0.729 |
> | 5 | ForecasterDirect (Ridge) | 0.0763 | 0.827 |
>
> The winning model (a pre-trained foundation model, Chronos-2-small, Apache-2.0 license) beat the seasonal-naive baseline on MAE across all 6 folds, and its MASE (0.58) is below 1 — meaning it also beats the simple one-step-naive reference. The 12-month forecast above was generated with this winning configuration.
>
> **Reasons for reasonable trust:**
> - It beat a real baseline over 6 independent backtest folds (not just one lucky window), which is the strongest level of evidence this workflow produces.
> - The series is clean: no missing values or date gaps, 204 monthly observations.
>
> **Caveats:**
> - The margin over the baseline is modest (beats the naive seasonal repeat by about an eighth on MAE). This is a "moderately better than naive" result, not a dramatically accurate one.
> - No prediction interval was computed, so there's no uncertainty band around these point forecasts — if you want one, I can rebuild the plan with an `interval` (e.g. `[0.1, 0.9]`).
> - Backtesting measures past accuracy; it doesn't guarantee the next 12 months behave like the historical folds.

### Final answer

> ## Forecast: `x` in `h2o.csv`, July 2008 – June 2009
>
> | Month | Forecast |
> |---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.003 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.031 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.084 |
> | 2008-10 | 1.184 |
> | 2008-11 | 1.171 |
> | 2008-12 | 1.281 |
> | 2009-01 | 1.281 |
> | 2009-02 | 0.682 |
> | 2009-03 | 0.791 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.761 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.844 |
> | 2009-06 | 0.912 |
>
> It rises through end of 2008, drops sharply in Feb 2009, then partially recovers — consistent with the series' recurring seasonal pattern.
>
> ## Can you trust it?
>
> Yes, reasonably — this forecast is backed by a proper model comparison, not just a single fit:
>
> - I backtested 6 folds of 12-month-ahead predictions (trained on data through 2003, tested on 2003–2008) and compared 5 candidate models against a seasonal-naive baseline.
> - The winner, a pretrained foundation model (**Chronos-2-small**, zero training needed), had **MAE 0.057**, beating the seasonal-naive baseline (0.066) by **13.7%** and the originally-recommended Ridge model (0.062) by 8%.
> - In relative terms, the backtest MAE is about **7% of the average forecast value** (MAPE ≈ 6.6%), which is a tight error band for a series with clear seasonality.
>
> Caveats:
> - This is a short, small (204-point) monthly series, so confidence intervals weren't computed and there's inherent uncertainty in any 12-month-ahead projection.
> - The backtest tests overlapping 12-month windows from 2003–2008; if the dynamics of 2008–2009 differ structurally from that period (e.g., a regime shift), accuracy could be worse than the historical backtest suggests.
>
> Overall: trustworthy as a decent point estimate, not as a precise guarantee — treat it as a working projection validated against a real baseline rather than an exact number.

> It reproduces the series' clear seasonal pattern: a rise toward year-end (Dec/Jan peak around 1.28) and a sharp drop into February (~0.68), consistent with the historical min/max range (0.336–1.257).
>
> ## Can you trust it?
>
> **Yes, reasonably** — this went through the full validation chain, not just a blind forecast:
>
> - I backtested 5 candidate models over 6 folds of 12 months each (holding out ~30% of the 204-observation history).
> - A pre-trained foundation model (**Chronos-2-small**, Apache-2.0 license) came out on top with MAE 0.057 (MAPE ≈ 6.7%), **beating the seasonal-naive baseline by 13.7%** — the key bar for trust, since a model that can't beat "repeat last year's value" isn't adding anything.
> - The Ridge model originally recommended (MAE 0.062) and an ARIMA model (MAE 0.064) were close behind but didn't beat the foundation model.
> - The forecast above comes from that winning configuration, not the default recommendation.
>
> Caveats worth keeping in mind:
> - The dataset is small (204 points), so the backtest's 6 folds give a reasonable but not huge sample of evidence.
> - No prediction intervals were computed in this run — the numbers above are point forecasts only. If you want uncertainty bounds, I can rerun with an interval (e.g. 80%).
> - This is univariate: no external/exogenous drivers were available or used.
>

### Final answer

> ## 12-month forecast for `x` (2008-07 to 2009-06)
>
> | Date | Forecast |
> |---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.003 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.031 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.084 |
> | 2008-10 | 1.184 |
> | 2008-11 | 1.171 |
> | 2008-12 | 1.281 |
> | 2009-01 | 1.281 |
> | 2009-02 | 0.682 |
> | 2009-03 | 0.791 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.761 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.844 |
> | 2009-06 | 0.912 |
>
> This follows the series' usual winter-peak / spring-trough seasonal pattern.
>
> ## Can you trust it?
>
> **Reasonably yes, with normal caveats.** I compared 5 candidate models via 6-fold backtesting (rolling 12-month windows over the last ~5 years of data) against a seasonal-naive baseline:
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE |
> |---|---|---|
> | 1 | **Chronos-2-small (foundation model)** ← used for forecast | **0.057** |
> | 2 | Ridge (ForecasterRecursive) | 0.062 |
> | 3 | ARIMA | 0.064 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.066 |
> | 5 | Ridge (ForecasterDirect) | 0.076 |
>
> The winning model beat the naive seasonal baseline by **13.7%** on MAE, and all top candidates beat it too — meaning there's real learnable structure beyond "repeat last year," and the model is capturing it. MAPE on backtests was ~6.7%, which is solid for this kind of series.
>
> Caveats to keep in mind:
> - Only 204 monthly observations (17 years) — a small dataset, so estimates have some uncertainty.
> - The margin over the naive baseline, while real, isn't huge — this series is highly seasonal and regular, so even simple methods do fairly well.
> - This is a point forecast without a prediction interval; if you want uncertainty bands around these 12 values, I can add one (e.g., an 80% interval) in a follow-up run.

> ## 24-hour forecast of `users`
>
> Data: hourly series from `data/bike.csv` (2012-10-02 to 2012-12-30 23:00). Forecaster: ForecasterRecursive + LGBMRegressor, trained on all 2,160 observations, exogenous columns (`holiday`, `weather`, `temp`) left out since no future values were given.
>
> **Predicted hourly users, 2012-12-31 00:00–23:00:**
>
> | Hour | Users | Hour | Users |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 00:00 | 26 | 12:00 | 70 |
> | 01:00 | 13 | 13:00 | 52 |
> | 02:00 | 11 | 14:00 | 44 |

> Mean ≈ 30 users/hour, with a clear morning peak around 11:00 and an overnight trough around 05:00.

> **Accuracy check (backtest, 27 folds, same plan):** MAE 59.8, MASE 0.73 — better than the one-step naive reference (values below 1 beat it), though the error is sizable relative to typical hourly counts (mean 216 over the full history, lower near this date). Treat the hour-by-hour shape as more reliable than the exact numbers.
>
> Note: this forecast excludes `holiday`, `weather`, and `temp`. If you can supply their expected values for Dec 31, I can rebuild the plan with exogenous variables, which may improve accuracy.

### Final answer

> ## Forecast (next 14 days, 2015‑01‑02 → 2015‑01‑15)
>
> The server profiled `items.csv` as 3 daily series (`item_1`, `item_2`, `item_3`, 400 observations each, no gaps/missing values). It compared two candidates over 9 backtest folds of 14 days each: `ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries` (LGBMRegressor) vs. `ForecasterFoundation` (Chronos‑2‑small, Apache‑2.0 license, weights downloaded from Hugging Face). **The foundation model won**, with a lower average MASE (0.79 vs. 1.11, 29.0% ahead per the comparison). The forecast below comes from that winning plan.

>
> ## Reliability per item
>
> These come from the 9‑fold backtest of the winning model (`out/comparison-4-64ef9e-best-metrics.csv`), measured by `mean_absolute_scaled_error` (MASE) — the error divided by a one‑step naive forecast on the training data; **below 1 beats that naive reference, above 1 does worse**:
>
> | Item | MASE | MAE | Reading |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 0.60 | 0.91 | Most reliable of the three — clearly beats the naive reference. |
> | item_3 | 0.77 | 2.97 | Reliable — beats the naive reference, though with a larger absolute error (this series has the widest range/highest variance). |
> | item_2 | 1.00 | 2.52 | Least reliable — essentially tied with just repeating the last observed value; treat its forecast with more caution. |
>
> Important caveats:
> - There was no seasonal-naive baseline for this comparison: with 3 pooled series, `ForecasterEquivalentDate` can't be ranked against a multi-series candidate, so the MASE-vs-1 reading above is the relevant reliability signal, not a "% better than baseline" number.
> - This is backtest accuracy (folds of historical 14-day windows), not an error measure on the actual future dates above — the standard caveat that backtest performance is informative but not a guarantee for any specific future window.
> - No prediction intervals were requested, so the table only shows point forecasts.

### Final answer

> ## Workflow
>
> Your data has 3 daily series (item_1, item_2, item_3, 400 days each, no gaps, no exogenous variables, 2013‑11‑28 to 2015‑01‑01). I compared a multi-series LightGBM forecaster against a foundation model (Chronos‑2‑small, Apache‑2.0 license, no training — it reads your raw history as context) over 9 backtest folds of 14 days each. **Chronos‑2‑small won** (average MASE 0.79 vs. 1.11 for LightGBM), so I used it for the final 14‑day forecast. Since this is multi-series data, there's no seasonal-naive baseline to compare against overall — reliability is judged per series by MASE (error relative to a naive "repeat last value" forecast; below 1 is better than naive, above 1 is worse).
>
> ## 14-day forecast (2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15)
>

>
> ## Reliability per item (MASE over the 9 backtest folds)
>
> | Item | MASE | Reading |
> |---|---|---|
> | **item_1** | 0.60 | Most reliable — beats the naive "repeat last value" forecast by a good margin. |
> | **item_3** | 0.77 | Reliable — clearly beats naive. |
> | **item_2** | 1.00 | Least reliable — essentially ties the naive forecast; the model adds little value here, and this series had the highest volatility (std 4.79 vs. mean 16.71) in the raw data. |
>
> No prediction intervals were computed for this run (the plan didn't request one), so these are point forecasts only — I can add an interval (e.g. 80%) if you'd like uncertainty bands.

> **Note on what this doesn't tell you:** this ranking says which model had lower backtest error, not *why* item_2 is harder to forecast — the server doesn't diagnose causes (e.g., anomalies, missing drivers). > ## 14-day forecast (2015-01-02 → 2015-01-15)
>
> Data: `data/items.csv`, 3 items, daily sales, 400 days of history (2013-11-28 to 2015-01-01).
>
> I compared a multi-series gradient-boosting model (LightGBM) against a foundation model (Chronos-2-small) via 9 backtest folds. **Chronos-2-small won** (MASE 0.79 vs. 1.11 overall), so the forecast below uses it. It's a pre-trained model (no training on your data), Apache-2.0 licensed, run locally.

>
> ## Reliability per item (from the backtest, measured over 9 folds of 14 days each)
>
> Reported as **mean_absolute_scaled_error (MASE)** — below 1 means the model beats a naive "repeat the last value" forecast on that series; above 1 means it does worse. Also showing MAPE for scale.
>
> | Item | MASE | MAPE | Reliability |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 0.60 | 4.8% | Most reliable — clearly beats the naive reference |
> | item_3 | 0.77 | 17.3% | Reliable — beats naive, but errors are a larger % of its values |
> | item_2 | 1.00 | 13.6% | Least reliable — about tied with just repeating the last known value |
>
> Caveats:
> - There's no baseline comparison for the *pooled* ranking (ForecasterEquivalentDate can't score several series at once), so reliability per item is judged via MASE on each series individually rather than a head-to-head "beats baseline" check.
> - Prediction intervals weren't requested, so these are point forecasts only — no uncertainty band.
> - These accuracy numbers come from past 14-day folds, not a guarantee for the specific next 14 days.

````text
import pandas as pd
from skforecast.foundation import FoundationModel, ForecasterFoundation

# Load data
data = pd.read_csv('<ws>/data/h2o.csv')

data['fecha'] = pd.to_datetime(data['fecha'])
data = data.set_index('fecha')
data = data.asfreq('MS')
data = data.sort_index()

series = data['x']

# Create foundation model (chronos-2-small)
estimator = FoundationModel(
    model_id       = 'autogluon/chronos-2-small',
    context_length = 8192,
)

# Create forecaster
forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=estimator)

# Fit (stores context only, no training)
forecaster.fit(series=series)

# Predict
steps = 12
predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
print(predictions)

````

> ## Results
>
> Your `data/h2o.csv` is a monthly series (204 obs, 1991‑07 to 2008‑06), no exogenous columns. I compared 5 configurations on the same 6 backtest folds (12-step horizon each), ranked by mean absolute error (MAE):
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE | MASE | Beats seasonal-naive baseline? |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | **ForecasterFoundation (Chronos‑2‑small)** | **0.0570** | 0.579 | Yes |
> | 2 | ForecasterRecursive (Ridge) | 0.0620 | 0.672 | Yes |
> | 3 | ForecasterStats (ARIMA) | 0.0638 | 0.648 | Yes |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.0661 | 0.729 | — |
> | 5 | ForecasterDirect (Ridge) | 0.0763 | 0.827 | No |
>
> **Best model: Chronos‑2‑small**, a pre-trained foundation model (no training needed, uses the whole 204-point history as context). It beat the seasonal-naive baseline by 13.7% and the next best model (Ridge) by 8.0%, all measured on identical cross-validation folds. Its license is Apache‑2.0 (Hugging Face: `autogluon/chronos-2-small`); weights download on first run.
>
> **12-month forecast (2008‑07 to 2009‑06) from the winning model:**

> This is a point forecast (no prediction interval was requested).

>

>
> # Fit (stores context only, no training)
> forecaster.fit(series=series)
>
> # Predict
> steps = 12
> predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
> print(predictions)

<details><summary>response (752 characters)</summary>

````text
import pandas as pd
from skforecast.foundation import FoundationModel, ForecasterFoundation

# Load data
data = pd.read_csv('<ws>/data/h2o.csv')

data['fecha'] = pd.to_datetime(data['fecha'])
data = data.set_index('fecha')
data = data.asfreq('MS')
data = data.sort_index()

series = data['x']

# Create foundation model (chronos-2-small)
estimator = FoundationModel(
    model_id       = 'autogluon/chronos-2-small',
    context_length = 8192,
)

# Create forecaster
forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=estimator)

# Fit (stores context only, no training)
forecaster.fit(series=series)

# Predict
steps = 12
predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
print(predictions)

````

</details>

### Final answer

> ## Comparison results
>
> Over 6 backtest folds (12-month horizon each, trained up to 2003-04), ranked by MAE:
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | **ForecasterFoundation (Chronos-2-small)** | 0.0570 | 0.579 |
> | 2 | ForecasterRecursive (Ridge) | 0.0620 | 0.672 |
> | 3 | ForecasterStats (ARIMA) | 0.0638 | 0.648 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.0661 | 0.729 |
> | 5 | ForecasterDirect (Ridge) | 0.0763 | 0.827 |
>
> **Winner: Chronos-2-small**, a pre-trained foundation model (no training — it forecasts directly from the raw history). It beats the seasonal-naive baseline by 13.7% and the next-best trained model (Ridge) by 8.0% on MAE. Its MASE of 0.579 means its error is about 58% of the one-step naive forecast on training data.
>
> Note: Chronos-2-small is licensed Apache-2.0 and downloads its weights from Hugging Face the first time it runs.
>
> The 12-month forecast (2008-07 to 2009-06) ranges roughly 0.68–1.28, mean ≈1.00 — no ground-truth comparison is possible since this is future data, not a holdout.
>
> ## Script to reproduce
>
> ```python

> )

>

> print(predictions)

````text
import pandas as pd
from skforecast.foundation import FoundationModel, ForecasterFoundation

# Load data
data = pd.read_csv('<ws>/data/h2o.csv')

data['fecha'] = pd.to_datetime(data['fecha'])
data = data.set_index('fecha')
data = data.asfreq('MS')
data = data.sort_index()

series = data['x']

# Create foundation model (chronos-2-small)
estimator = FoundationModel(
    model_id       = 'autogluon/chronos-2-small',
    context_length = 8192,
)

# Create forecaster
forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=estimator)

# Fit (stores context only, no training)
forecaster.fit(series=series)

# Predict
steps = 12
predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
print(predictions)

````

### Final answer

> ## Results
>
> I compared 5 forecasting approaches on `data/h2o.csv` (monthly series "x", 204 observations), backtested over 6 folds of 12-month horizons:
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | **ForecasterFoundation (Chronos-2-small)** | **0.0570** | 0.579 |
> | 2 | ForecasterRecursive + Ridge | 0.0620 | 0.672 |
> | 3 | ForecasterStats (ARIMA) | 0.0638 | 0.648 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.0661 | 0.729 |
> | 5 | ForecasterDirect + Ridge | 0.0763 | 0.827 |
>
> **Best model: Chronos-2-small (a foundation/pretrained time-series model)**, beating the next-best (Ridge) by 8% and the seasonal-naive baseline by 13.7% on mean absolute error. It requires no training — it forecasts directly from the raw series.
>
> Note: this model downloads its weights from Hugging Face on first run (Apache-2.0 license, permissive for commercial use).
>
> Here's the script to reproduce the winning forecast:
>
> ```python

>

> data = data.sort_index()
>
> series = data['x']
>
> # Create foundation model (chronos-2-small)
> estimator = FoundationModel(
>     model_id       = 'autogluon/chronos-2-small',
>     context_length = 8192,
> )
>
> # Create forecaster
> forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=estimator)
>
> # Fit (stores context only, no training)
> forecaster.fit(series=series)
>
> # Predict next 12 months
> steps = 12
> predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
> print(predictions)
> ```
>

### Final answer

> ## Summary
>
> **Setup:** `users` from `bike_users.csv` — hourly data, 2160 observations (2012-10-02 to 2012-12-30), no gaps. Plan: `ForecasterRecursive` + `LGBMRegressor`, 48 lags (as requested), plus window features (mean/std over 3h, mean over 24h and 168h) and calendar features (hour, day of week, weekend). 80% prediction interval ([0.1, 0.9]) via bootstrapping. Metric: MAE (as requested).
>
> **Backtest** (27 folds, 24-step horizon each, trained once on the first 70% of data, no refit):
> - **MAE = 66.24** over the backtested period (2012-12-04 to 2012-12-30)
> - This is a backtest without a baseline comparison, so treat it as a standalone accuracy measure, not a "beats naive" claim.
>
> **Forecast — next 24 hours (2012-12-31 00:00 to 23:00):**

### Final answer

> ## Setup
>
> - **Data:** `bike_users.csv` — 2160 hourly observations of `users`, 2012-10-02 to 2012-12-30, no gaps or missing values.
> - **Model:** `ForecasterRecursive` + `LGBMRegressor`, 48 lags (as requested), plus window features (mean/std of last 3h, mean of last 24h and 168h) and calendar features (hour, day of week, weekend).
> - **Metric:** MAE (as requested).
> - **Intervals:** 80% (quantiles [0.1, 0.9]), via bootstrapping.
>
> ## Backtest
>
> 27 folds of 24-hour horizons, trained once on the first 1512 observations (through 2012-12-03 23:00), no refitting across folds.
>
> **MAE = 66.24** (users/hour), over predictions ranging roughly 3–719 (mean ≈ 195, matching the data's own mean/std of 216/202). This is a single configuration's backtest, not compared against a baseline, so I can't say how it stacks up against a naive forecast — only report the raw MAE.
>
> ## Forecast: next 24 hours (2012-12-31 00:00 to 23:00)
>
> Trained on all 2160 observations. Predicted `users` range from ~6 to ~199 (mean ≈ 89), with 80% intervals roughly ±25–75 around each point depending on the hour. Full predictions with lower/upper bounds are in:
> `<ws>/out/forecast-5-d90798-predictions.csv`
>
> Note the forecast mean (≈89) is noticeably lower than the backtest's historical prediction mean (≈195) — this is New Year's Eve day, and lower demand is plausible, but the server doesn't explain *why*; it's just what the model, trained on the full history, output. Treat the intervals as estimates, not guarantees.

### Final answer

> ## Results
>
> **Data:** `data/h2o.csv` — monthly series `x`, 204 observations (1991-07 to 2008-06), no exogenous variables, no missing values.
>
> **Setup:** Compared 5 candidate models via 6-fold rolling backtest (12-step horizon per fold, initial training through 2003-04-01), ranked by MSE, with MAE also computed.
>
> ### Leaderboard (ranked by MSE)
>
> | Rank | Model | Estimator | MSE | MAE |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | ForecasterFoundation | Chronos-2-small | **0.00527** | **0.05701** |
> | 2 | ForecasterRecursive | Ridge | 0.00586 | 0.06198 |
> | 3 | ForecasterStats | ARIMA | 0.00613 | 0.06382 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | — | 0.00666 | 0.06607 |
> | 5 | ForecasterDirect | Ridge | 0.00918 | 0.07628 |
>
> The winner, **Chronos-2-small** (a pre-trained foundation model, Apache-2.0 license, downloaded from Hugging Face — no training performed), beats the seasonal-naive baseline by 20.9% on MSE and leads on MAE too. ForecasterDirect/Ridge was the only candidate to underperform the baseline.
>
> ### 12-month forecast (using the winning model)
>
> | Date | Forecast |
> |---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.0025 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.0310 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.0837 |

> | 2009-03 | 0.7911 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.7609 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.8435 |

>
> Full predictions are saved at `out/forecast-6-eba148-predictions.csv`; the leaderboard and per-fold metrics are in `out/comparison-4-eba148-leaderboard.csv` and `out/comparison-4-eba148-best-metrics.csv`.
>
> Note: this ranking reflects which model had the lowest backtest error over these 6 folds — it doesn't explain *why* (e.g., seasonality or trend handling), since the server doesn't measure causes, only accuracy.

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> Before running this, I want to flag the cost. A true "retrain-every-step" 24h-ahead backtest over 2 years of hourly data produces **220 folds and 220 separate model trainings** (LGBM refit every day), which the server flags as a `LongTrainingWarning` — it can take several minutes.
>
> Options:
> 1. **Run it as-is** (220 fits, refit every fold) — most faithful to "retrain every time new data arrives."
> 2. **Retrain weekly instead of daily** (`refit=7`, i.e. every 7 folds) — ~32 fits, still captures regular retraining, much cheaper, and realistically closer to how you'd run this in production (daily retrains of a tree model on 24h-ahead data add little vs. weekly).
> 3. **Fewer folds** via a larger `fold_stride` or later `initial_train_size` — cheaper but evaluates fewer of the 220 daily windows, so less representative of the full 2 years.
>
> Which would you like? If you want the full 220-fit daily-retrain backtest, just confirm and I'll run it.

**Turn 2**

> Here's how the 24-hour-ahead forecast would have performed over the two years, evaluated with a model retrained weekly (expanding window) and re-tested on 220 daily, 24-hour-ahead windows from 2012-05-26 onward (the first 70% of data used as initial training):
>
> | Metric | Value |
> |---|---|
> | Mean Absolute Error | 48.4 users |
> | Root context: Mean Squared Error | 6303.2 (RMSE ≈ 79.4 users) |
> | Mean Absolute Percentage Error | 47.5% |
> | Mean Absolute Scaled Error | 0.74 |
>
> **Reading these:** actual hourly ridership in this data ranges 1–977 with a mean of ~188, so a typical 24h-ahead prediction is off by about 48 riders. The MASE of 0.74 means the model's error is smaller than that of a one-step naive reference (repeating the previous hour's value, measured on the training data) — it does **not** mean it beats a seasonal-naive baseline, since no baseline was computed here.
>
> **Setup notes:**
> - Model: LGBMRegressor via `ForecasterRecursive`, retrained every 7 folds (≈ weekly) rather than every single day, to keep training cost reasonable (32 trainings instead of 220) while still evaluating all 220 daily 24h-ahead windows.
> - Training window expands over time (not fixed-size), matching how you'd accumulate history in production.
>
> If you want to know whether this actually beats a simple seasonal-naive forecast (e.g., "same hour, same day of week as last week"), I can run a `compare` against that baseline — just let me know.

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> ## Results: 24-hour-ahead forecast, retrained daily (as in production)
>
> **Setup:** LightGBM recursive forecaster, trained on the first ~70% of the data (through 2012-05-26), then evaluated on the remaining ~7 months by rolling forward one day at a time — retraining from scratch on all data seen so far before each new 24-hour forecast (220 retrain cycles total).
>
> | Model | MAE (users/hour) | MAPE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **LightGBM (daily retrain)** | **47.4** | 47.1% | 0.73 |
> | Seasonal-naive baseline (same hour last week) | 80.3 | 68.5% | 1.25 |
>
> **Takeaways:**
> - The model beats the naive "same hour as last week" baseline by **41%** — so it's genuinely learning useful patterns (recent demand, time-of-day, day-of-week), not just repeating seasonality.
> - On average, a 24-hour-ahead forecast is off by about **47 users** out of a mean of ~188/hour — a relative error around 47%. That's moderate: usable for capacity planning but not precise enough for tight operational decisions.
> - Errors are heavily skewed toward high-demand hours (MSE is large relative to MAE), meaning the biggest misses happen during peak usage, which is usually when accuracy matters most.
>
> Predictions and per-fold metrics are saved to CSV if you want to dig into specific days (e.g., `backtest-4-dde3e3-metrics.csv`) — want me to look at where the errors are largest (weekday vs weekend, rush hour, etc.)?

**Turn 2**

> With weekly retraining (32 fits instead of 220), results are virtually identical:
>
> | Model | MAE | MAPE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | LightGBM (**weekly** retrain) | 48.4 | 47.5% | 0.74 |
> | LightGBM (daily retrain, previous run) | 47.4 | 47.1% | 0.73 |
> | Seasonal-naive baseline | 80.3 | 68.5% | 1.25 |
>
> Retraining weekly instead of daily costs ~7x less to run and still beats the naive baseline by ~40%, with only a 2% increase in MAE. That's the cheaper, still-production-realistic option — I'd recommend it over daily retraining.

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> ## Results: 24-hour-ahead forecast, retrained daily
>
> Simulated production over the full two years: train on data up to a point, forecast the next 24 hours, then retrain and roll forward one day at a time (expanding window, LightGBM, lags + rolling/calendar features chosen from the data). This gave **220 daily retrain-and-forecast cycles**, covering late May through December 2012 (the first ~70% of data seeds the initial model).
>
> | | MAE | MAPE | vs. seasonal-naive baseline |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Model | **47.4 users** | 47.1% | **beats it by 41%** |
> | Baseline (repeats last day/week) | 80.3 users | 68.5% | — |
>
> **Takeaway:** a daily-retrained 24h-ahead model is off by about 47 riders/hour on average (mean hourly demand is ~188, so roughly 25% of the mean), and comfortably beats a naive "same hour as before" forecast. The 47% MAPE looks large mostly because low-usage hours (near-zero riders) inflate percentage error — the absolute error is the more reliable number here.
>
> Predictions and per-fold metrics are saved to:
> - `out/backtest-4-58d6ba-predictions.csv`
> - `out/backtest-4-58d6ba-metrics.csv`
>
> Want me to break the error down by time of day/season, or try a different retrain cadence (e.g., weekly instead of daily) to see the accuracy/cost tradeoff?

**Turn 2**

> ## Weekly retrain vs. daily retrain
>
> | Retrain cadence | Retrainings | MAE | MAPE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Daily (every 24h) | 220 | 47.4 | 47.1% |
> | **Weekly (every 7 days)** | **32** | **48.4** | **47.5%** |
>
> Retraining weekly instead of daily cuts the number of model trainings by ~7x (220 → 32) while only costing about **1 extra rider/hour of error** (+2% MAE) — a good tradeoff for production. The 24-hour-ahead forecast is still accurate and stable with much less retraining overhead.
>
> Predictions and metrics saved to:
> - `out/backtest-8-58d6ba-predictions.csv`
> - `out/backtest-8-58d6ba-metrics.csv`

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> ## Results
>
> Simulating production — the model retrains daily (expanding training window, 220 retrainings) and each time forecasts the next 24 hours — over the second half of the two years (2012-05-26 to 2012-12-31, ~220 days):
>
> | Candidate | MAE (users/hr) | MAPE | RMSE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **LGBMRegressor** (winner) | **47.4** | **47.1%** | 6106 |
> | Baseline (seasonal naive, same hour last week) | 80.3 | 68.5% | 18047 |
>
> - The trained model beats the seasonal-naive baseline by **~41%** on MAE.
> - On average, a 24-hour-ahead forecast is off by about **47 riders/hour**, against a mean demand of ~188 riders/hour (MAPE ≈ 47%). Errors are naturally largest during demand spikes, since RMSE (6106 → ~78 in the same units) is much higher than MAE, indicating a tail of larger misses (e.g., unusual weather/event days).
>
> **Setup**: LGBMRegressor via skforecast's `ForecasterRecursive`, lags up to 337h, rolling-window features (3h/24h/168h means), and calendar features (hour, day-of-week, weekend, month). Cross-validation retrained the model every 24 hours on an expanding window (true production simulation, not a single train/test split).
>
> Predictions and per-fold metrics are saved to CSV at `comparison-5-90c731-best-predictions.csv` and `backtest-4-90c731-metrics.csv` in the output directory if you want to inspect specific days or plot the forecast vs. actuals.

**Turn 2**

> ## Results (weekly retrain, cheaper)
>
> | Candidate | MAE | MAPE | RMSE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **LGBMRegressor** (winner) | **48.4** | **47.5%** | 6303 |
> | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 80.3 | 68.5% | 18047 |
>
> Virtually identical to the daily-retrain run (MAE 47.4 → 48.4, a ~2% difference) but at **32 model fits instead of 220** — retraining weekly captures almost all the accuracy of retraining daily. The model still beats the seasonal-naive baseline by **~40%**.
>
> **Bottom line:** a 24-hour-ahead forecast, retrained weekly in production, would have had a mean absolute error of ~48 riders/hour (MAPE ~47%) over the back half of the two-year dataset.

> ## Result
>
> Trained a `ForecasterRecursive` + `Ridge` model (lags [1,9,10,11,12,13,14], window features for mean/std, calendar features month/quarter) on `data/h2o.csv` (monthly series `x`, 1991-07 to 2008-06, 204 observations), then evaluated it on the last 24 observations (2006-07-01 to 2008-06-01), which the model had never seen during training.
>

>
> | Metric | Value |
> |---|---|
> | MAE | 0.0520 |

The MASE of 0.553 means the error is about half that of a naive one-step "repeat the last value" forecast computed on the training data — note this reference is *not* the seasonal-naive baseline used by `compare`, so it shouldn't be read as beating that specific baseline.
>

> `ForecasterRecursive` + Ridge (the default recommendation) failed to backtest: its rolling window features reach back across the `2004-10-01` gap, which Ridge can't handle. Switching to LGBMRegressor (tolerates missing values) worked, MAE ≈ 0.080. A `compare` run then found a stronger candidate: **ForecasterFoundation** (Chronos-2-small, a pre-trained foundation model, no training needed) with **MAE ≈ 0.060** (24% better), so I used that for the final forecast. No seasonal-naive baseline could be computed because of the missing values, so this is judged by backtest MAE alone, not a baseline comparison.

>
> I ran a `compare` across 6 backtest folds (12-step horizon each), benchmarking the foundation model against a seasonal-naive baseline, an ARIMA model, and two Ridge-based forecasters:

Its `mean_absolute_scaled_error` of 0.58 means its average error is about 58% the size of a one-step naive forecast's error on the training data (that reference point, not the baseline above).
